title: The Golden Circle
hook: 3 labels can still blur the stake: if no behavior answers them, the slogan wins.
counterintuition: The visible thing does not lead; it pays the price of the reason. Apple Inc., the company founded in 1976 and based in Cupertino, makes that plain when Macintosh serves a challenger belief.
tryThisNow: When a message starts with what you made, move 1 reason above it in 5 minutes and cut the line no behavior can prove.
keyTakeaway: Use the Golden Circle as an order you can inspect: move WHY before HOW, let WHAT show the claim, and keep each hard detail in its own case.

breakdown.fastRead: 3 labels look clean on a startup founder's draft: WHY, HOW, WHAT. The first label names why the work matters. The second names how the reason shows up. The third names what people can see. Yet the draft still feels thin, because the visible thing is doing too much. Apple Inc., the company founded in 1976 and based in Cupertino, makes the risk plain. Macintosh, the visible product in that account, is not a magic opener. It works only when a challenger belief has already priced the promise. If the founder starts with product facts, the facts have to invent meaning. If the founder starts with WHY, the facts can prove a claim. Who asks, and where can they see the answer? That is the move.
breakdown.deepRead:
A founder's first draft has a price. It lists Apple Inc., 1976, Cupertino, and Macintosh, then hopes the list will do the thinking. The Golden Circle is the plain order WHY before HOW before WHAT. It does not ask you to sound grand. It asks you to put the reason where the later proof can serve it.

Use restraint. When the person already shares the reason and only needs the action, give the action first. When a true detail belongs to one source, keep it there. Cupertino is a hard fact inside the Apple account, not a spare part for any paragraph that needs weight.

Price the default before you copy it. The default says, "Lead with the thing; people will infer the belief." That costs you twice. The thing has to prove itself and explain itself, while the belief stays vague. She moves one reason above the product line and keeps the product as what the reader can inspect. The sentence gets less flashy. It gets more honest.

A second anchor stops the Apple material from turning into a charm. At Kitty Hawk on December 17, 1903, Orville Wright and Wilbur Wright flew. Their story is not Apple with wings. It puts aim and staying power ahead of credentials. That contrast matters because one vivid example can show an idea, but it cannot price the default across a new setting.

You can run the same small move without title power. Pick one live message. Ask, what is the reason, what is the way, and what visible thing should carry the proof? If the line has no answer, do not make it warmer. Move the reason up.
breakdown.fullRead:
A failed paragraph shows the other side. Cupertino had been moved into a Wright brothers note because the place sounded exact. The sentence stayed factual in one sense and became false in use. A hard detail is a promise tied to one source. Move it and you may make the whole claim feel made up.

The Golden Circle helps only when the parts keep their jobs. WHY names the belief. HOW names the way the belief shows up. WHAT names the thing people can see. Blend them and you cannot tell what must be paid for, who pays it, or where the proof should sit.

Apple Inc is the first visible setting, not a mascot. Its 1976 start and Cupertino base let you inspect the claim. Macintosh gives the WHAT a body. The product does not lead; the reason gives the product a job. That job is narrow: show that the challenger belief was not just a line in the opening.

The Wright brothers give the comparison a new surface. Orville Wright is a factual token Apple does not have, and Wilbur Wright keeps the story from sounding like one lone inventor. December 17, 1903 and Kitty Hawk do not make them more Apple-like. They make the difference visible. If you stamp every example with the same shape, the price is trust; real material starts to sound invented.

Martin Luther King Jr., the civil-rights speaker at the Lincoln Memorial in Washington, DC on August 28, 1963, marks a limit. The point is not that every public cause, company, and flight story works the same way. The point is that belief can attract people before a policy list when the setting supports that read. The Lincoln Memorial is a boundary marker in plain sight. It tells you where not to stretch.

Your own moment can be smaller. You do not need a stage or a title. When a project update opens with the thing you shipped, ask what reason that thing is meant to show. When a method line sounds neat, ask what belief gives it a job. When a detail feels useful only because it is sharp, ask whose story it belongs to.

The cost of skipping this step is not vague. A product has to act like a cause. A place becomes a borrowed badge. A date turns into a stamp. Then the message may sound firm while every unowned promise costs another week of pretending.

Use the order as a question, not a chant. What belief comes first? What way makes it visible? What thing can bear the price? If you cannot answer, do less, not more. Lift the reason, keep the detail home, and let the visible act earn its keep.

examples.title: Sylvia Prices The First Draft

planSpec.stakes: a promise that cannot yet be proved
planSpec.requiredBeat: Apple Inc. becomes evidence, not decoration

examples.scenario: Why does a pitch with Apple Inc. facts still feel thin? Imagine startup founder Sylvia in a parked car as the dashboard light blinks. Her before line has four true pieces: the company, 1976, Cupertino, Macintosh. The early signal no one flagged is the missing reason. After the move, the same four pieces sit under one challenger belief, but behavior still has to prove it.
examples.whatToDo: Price the default: move the reason above the four company details, then cut any product line that has no behavior behind it.
examples.whyItMatters: She leaves with a cleaner question, not a finished win. Four facts now support one claim, and the open risk is whether behavior can bear it.

examples.title: Sylvia Drops The Stamp

planSpec.stakes: one vivid story doing too much
planSpec.requiredBeat: the Apple Inc. thread earns its own proof

examples.scenario: Founder Sylvia states the standard: "One visible fact earns one reason." Suppose she wants the Wright brothers to mirror Apple Inc. with a neat place-and-year shell. She keeps Orville and Wilbur tied to Kitty Hawk on December 17, 1903. The move works because contrast replaces a stamp. The cost is a simpler page with fewer easy parallels.
examples.whatToDo: Make the contrast: keep the Wright brothers on their own facts, drop the Apple-shaped shell, and state what changed between the two anchors.
examples.whyItMatters: She pays with neatness. The lesson gains trust because the second anchor is no longer a stamped copy of the first one.

examples.title: Jerome Catches The List

planSpec.requiredBeat: belief goes before the visible list

examples.scenario: Community organizer Jerome is cutting the policy list before a civic forum when the microphone hums. The demand had already been made: belief before visible list. He is about to miss it by treating Martin Luther King Jr., the speaker at the Lincoln Memorial in Washington, DC on August 28, 1963, as a famous close. Jerome catches the error late and moves the belief line above the policy items.
examples.whatToDo: Jerome gives the command: move belief before the list, keep the public-cause setting intact, and cut any line that makes fame do the work.
examples.whyItMatters: Jerome's warning is direct: skip the order and a public cause shrinks into bullets; keep belief first and the list has a job.

examples.title: Brock Repairs The Drift

planSpec.stakes: true facts used in the wrong place
planSpec.requiredBeat: hard specifics stay inside their source

examples.scenario: At the workshop check-in, founder Sylvia names the miss after it has already played out. Suppose she had moved Cupertino into another example because a real place felt strong. The after was worse than the before: one true Apple Inc. detail made the other section look fake. She moves Cupertino back and leaves one open question: which company behavior will prove the reason?
examples.whatToDo: Start with the skipped cost: keep Cupertino inside Apple Inc., then replace the borrowed detail with a fact from the source at hand.
examples.whyItMatters: Sylvia's repair makes the cost plain. A true fact in the wrong story weakens both stories and leaves the reader unsure what to trust.

questions.prompt: Your public-cause draft already uses Apple Inc. well, then adds Martin Luther King Jr. What is the single best use of the new scene?
choices: Treat the civil-rights scene as proof that every organization should follow the Apple pattern in the same way.
Use Washington, D.C. and August 28, 1963 to expose a nearby misconception without repeating Apple Inc.
Mention Martin Luther King Jr. for color, then let the paragraph teach the same Apple lesson again.
questions.explanation: The King anchor should change cast and setting so a nearby error is visible. The same-way option overreaches; the new scene should not restamp Apple Inc.

questions.prompt: When volunteer Yann rewrites a nonprofit donor page and shortens WHY, HOW, WHAT to one purpose word before sending it, what breaks first?
choices: The shorter word still works if people can remember it and the message feels easier to repeat.
The three jobs collapse, so reason, method, and visible result can no longer be sorted.
Only the WHAT gets weaker; the WHY and HOW keep their jobs without the third term.
questions.explanation: The framework works because each word has a job. The memory-word option is tempting, but it trades useful sorting for a slogan the reader cannot inspect.

questions.prompt: Suppose a founder opens a pitch with Apple Inc. as a colorful opener, then never links it to behavior. What should change?
choices: Keep Apple Inc. as background after the broader purpose claim, since the familiar name already adds force.
Let 1976 settle the claim and stop asking whether visible choices carry the reason.
Make Apple Inc. carry evidence by asking which visible choices show the reason.
questions.explanation: Apple Inc. is evidence only when visible behavior can show the reason. A bare founding year feels firm, yet it cannot answer what the belief costs in action.

questions.prompt: After Brock sends a product launch note that puts HOW first and saves WHY for the end, the update reads tidy but vague. What is likely downstream?
choices: The tactic carries the reason's job, so the note can sound neat while the premise stays weak.
The order remains a style choice if all three parts appear somewhere in the note and the ending names a belief.
The method gains trust because readers often prefer concrete process before belief.
questions.explanation: WHY has to frame HOW. The all-parts-somewhere choice misses the mechanism, since a late reason leaves the tactic carrying a job it cannot do.

questions.prompt: A training guide gives broad purpose advice but drops Apple Inc., the Wright brothers, and Martin Luther King Jr. Which flaw matters most?
choices: Named anchors should replace purpose words, so the guide should remove the reason and keep only famous material.
The guide loses its checkable ground; the three anchors carry details that keep the lesson from floating.
The advice can stand if the purpose sentence sounds sincere and the examples would only add color.
questions.explanation: The three anchors make the claim checkable. The famous-material choice fails in the other direction: it drops purpose instead of grounding it.

questions.prompt: In a comparison note for a workshop, a facilitator adds Orville Wright rather than another Apple Inc. detail. Why does that help?
choices: Orville Wright gives the Wright brothers their own token, so contrast can replace a generic success pattern.
The facilitator can now reuse Apple's year-place rhythm, which makes both stories easier to match in a tidy comparison for listeners.
The comparison becomes stronger by treating the flight story as a business example.
questions.explanation: Orville Wright gives the Wright brothers a token Apple does not share. The year-place rhythm answer fails because copied shape makes real material look stamped.

questions.prompt: Before a facilitator in a short class claims the idea carries beyond Apple Inc. after only one company story, which step is sound?
choices: Bring in the Wright brothers at Kitty Hawk on December 17, 1903 and compare what repeats.
Let Apple Inc. settle the model, because one clear story can prove the pattern by itself.
Add another anchor only after the transfer claim is already treated as settled.
questions.explanation: The second anchor lets comparison reveal what repeats. Apple-only proof is too broad; one example can illustrate, but it cannot compare.

questions.prompt: Your civic speech draft for a local campaign treats the Lincoln Memorial like a company office while sorting the message. What has gone wrong?
choices: The strong place detail now lets the same use apply across organizations and causes.
The place detail mainly adds vividness, so the message can stay broad without a limit.
The limit has been erased; the detail should mark where the move changes by venue.
questions.explanation: The Lincoln Memorial marks a limit, not a license to flatten settings. The vividness option misses the warning that venue changes the mechanism.

questions.prompt: During a repair pass, a writer moves Cupertino into a Wright brothers paragraph because the place is real. Which principle should stop him?
choices: The issue is mostly order; Cupertino only needs to appear after WHY and HOW.
A verified place can strengthen a weak paragraph when the sentence remains true and the source label looks clear.
A hard detail must stay with the source that can prove it, or grounding turns false.
questions.explanation: Cupertino belongs to Apple Inc. The verified-place choice is the trap: a real detail misleads when it is attached to the wrong source.

reviewCards.front: What is the first move when a message opens with WHAT?
reviewCards.back: Move WHY above the thing made. The method and visible proof can help only after the reason gives them a job.

reviewCards.front: Why does HOW need WHY in front of it?
reviewCards.back: HOW is a way of serving the reason. If it comes first, it has to explain the premise and prove the method at the same time.

reviewCards.front: What should happen to a sharp detail like Cupertino?
reviewCards.back: Keep it inside the source that can prove it. A true detail moved for force becomes false grounding.

reviewCards.front: When is the full WHY-first order too much?
reviewCards.back: When the reason is already shared and the person only needs the visible action. Then give the WHAT plainly and save the frame for real confusion.

reviewCards.front: What does a second anchor add that one strong example cannot?
reviewCards.back: It lets you compare. One example can show the idea, but a second source lets you see what repeats and what changes.

reviewCards.front: What warning sits under broad purpose advice?
reviewCards.back: Purpose words need checkable anchors. Without named facts and visible behavior, the advice may sound true while no one can inspect it.

implementationPlan.title: Move The Reason Up
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Use the Golden Circle as an order for one live message. Put the reason first, name the way it shows up, and let the visible thing carry proof. Keep hard details with the source that can prove them.

ifThenPlans.plan: If your first line names the thing you made, then move one reason above it.
If a true detail sounds useful outside its source, then move it back to the source that can prove it.
If the reason is already shared, then give the needed WHAT first.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Teach one person for 10 minutes: move WHY ahead of HOW and WHAT in your own words, then ask for one behavior that would prove the promise.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each week, measure one number: how many live messages began with a reason before the method or proof. Move the worst miss and count again.

memorableLines.text: Price the default before you copy it.
memorableLines.why: It gives the reader a short command for the cost-speak move.

memorableLines.text: The product does not lead; the reason gives the product a job.
memorableLines.why: It reverses the habit of letting the visible offer explain itself.

memorableLines.text: A hard detail is a promise tied to one source.
memorableLines.why: It redefines a factual detail as a source-bound promise.
